item.title: [Concurrency] Introduce a split continuation This PR implements [SE-0564: ...
item.description:
[Concurrency] Introduce a split continuation
This PR implements [SE-0564: Split continuations](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0564-split-continuations.md).
`withContinuation`'s synchronous-body form couples creating a continuation with awaiting it. When creating continuations it is common to want to setup cancellation and escalation handlers as well. With the current form the only way to do this is by setting up the handlers around the `withContinuation` method. However, this leads to hard to handle races where the cancellation handler can be called before the continuation is even created. Furthermore, it also makes state tracking harder and forces developers to create an id or another token that can be used as an identity for the continuation and the handlers.
This PR adds a split form of `withContinuation` whose body is `async` and receives both halves of one continuation. The existing `Continuation` that is used for resuming and a new `ContinuationWaiter` that is used for waiting. The waiter is a `~Copyable` and `~Escapable` type that must be `wait()`ed on by the end of the `withContinuation` scope. It enforces this invariant by trapping in `deinit` similar to what `Continuation` does. Its `wait` methods can install cancellation and escalation handlers that are only active while the task is suspended on the continuation.
In addition to this, the PR adds new `resumeSynchronously` methods to `Continuation`, `UnsafeContinuation` and `CheckedContinuation` where we pass in the execution context. This is meant to be used by executors so that they can resume continuations and donate their context if possible. To support this, regular continuations now record the executor the task suspends on instead of always the generic executor.
Lastly, priority escalation handlers, including the one of `withTaskPriorityEscalationHandler`, are now called once with the task's current priority when they are installed. This closes a race where an escalation that happens before the handler is installed is never reported.
Since this is re-using the existing `Continuation` type we need to make sure that existing code that handles them keeps working if they get a `Continuation` passed that was created by the new `withContinuation` method. There are a few technical challenges with that, that influence the implementation:
- A split continuation cannot put the task into an awaiting state right away. Instead this only happens when the waiter is `wait()`ed on. - The current continuation has a reference to the existing task and assumes the offset of the resume context from it. A split continuation needs to match this so that an ordinary `resume` works. This is achieved by laying out the split continuation header similar to how an `AsyncTask` is laid out so that the existing `resume` methods continue to work. - The split continuation header has a marker in the beginning allowing the resume methods to identify it.

item.title: [Sema] Diagnose likely-unsound script var forward references Emit an error...
item.description:
[Sema] Diagnose likely-unsound script var forward references
Emit an error for a forward reference to a global script-mode variable that is likely to be unsound. This handles cases where the variable is stored, and the reference is made at the top level before the declaration. Such uses would otherwise have likely read uninitialized memory.
The only way such a reference could have been used in a sound way is by also initializing it before declaration, e.g:
``` x = 1 print(x) let x: Int ```
But source compatibility testing has shown this to be incredibly rare, testing across both the source compat suite and internal Swift projects at Apple has only turned up a single case so far.
Uses within closures and functions are unfortunately more common so cannot be outright banned for now.
Note that this checking doesn't help with cross-file cases, ultimately we still need to properly fix script-mode variables such that they are consistently treated as either local or global variables. Such a change will be quite source breaking though, this patch at least allows us to diagnose the majority of cases in the mean time.
### Why not diagnose in SIL?
SILGen already emits `mark_uninitialized` and `mark_function_escape` instructions for script-mode variables which allows use-before-init to be diagnosed by DefiniteInitialization, however this only works when the use actually follows the declaration. In principe we could adjust the SILGen here to emit these mark instructions at the start of `main`, which would let us more precisely diagnose _only_ the unsound cases. However the fact that we allow these forward references is also generally problematic in Sema, e.g:
``` print(a) guard let b = 3 as Int? else {} let a = b ```
This currently crashes the compiler since the forward reference to `a` kicks lazy type-checking, which type-checks the statement condition. This then results in us attempting to type-check the condition multiple times. Such code would already be invalid if in a local context such as a function. In principe we could defensively guard against these cases, but I would rather just eliminate them entirely.
Forum post to follow.

item.description:
[SE-0551, stdlib] Form a single-element Span over a value (#88152)
Form a Span over the value in any binding, and a MutableSpan over any mutable binding.
Implements the change proposed in [SE-0551](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0551-span-of-one.md).
Addresses rdar://156165923 and rdar://167869600
